## Goals

1. Develop an understanding of branching in `git`.
2. Practice using `git branch` to work asynchronously.
3. Practice using `git push` and `git pull` to create pull requests and synchronize work.

## Before class

Working on your final projects will require collaboration with `git`.
In [Lab 5](lab5-codereview.qmd) we practiced creating pull requests primarily as a means to review each other's work.
This assignment closes the collaboration loop by showing you how to work asynchronously with **branches** in `git`.

The following figure summarizes the various actions your team will need to collectively understand in order to collaborate effortlessly.

![Credit: [*Research Software Engineering with Python*, Chapter 6, Figure 6.5](https://third-bit.com/py-rse/git-cmdline.html#fig:git-cmdline-remote); licensed under CC-BY 4.0](assets/git-workflow.png)

### Review

#### `git status`

- Tells us the current state of the repository.
- Reports what is tracked, what is untracked, and which tracked files have changed.
- **When To Use This**:
    + Starting or resuming work on your repository.
    + Before you `git add` files.
    + Before you `git commit` to ensure everything you need is staged.

#### `git diff`

- Shows changes in any tracked files. That means (i) file was staged and part of a commit at some point, and (ii) you modified that file again but have not staged or commited it yet.
- Also have `git diff --staged` if you need to compare after you `git add` files.
- **When To Use This**:
    + After modifying a file that was staged.
    + Before you `git commit` to quickly check your changes.
    + To compare differences across commits.

#### `git add`

- This stages a file prior to a commit.
- Remember that editing a file merely changes your working tree (the directory). Staging prepares files(s) to be part of a commit; a discrete change in the repository itself.
- **When To Use This**:
    + After completing changes to a file or set of files.
    + After making additional changes to already staged files; i.e. you continued editing after `git add` because you forgot something.
    + To prepare the next commit.

#### `git commit`

- This moves staged changes (anything touched by `git add`) to your repository's commit history.
- Always include a succinct and informative message as part of your commits. **This will be important for your collaborators**.
- Make small changes based on discrete tasks and commit them. Several students have been diligent about making a commit after solving a problem on the assignments.
- **When To Use This**:
    + After completing a particular task.
    + Whenever you need to prepare and share your work with your collaborators.

#### `git log`

- This lets us review a repository's commit history.
- `git log` has been sufficient for our purposes. Now we need to use its various options.
- `git log --stat --summary`: Condensed overview of each commit, which lists the files that were changed in addition to the usual commit information.
- `git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all`: Displays commit history, including different branches, in a graph-like display. Might be fairly linear in the beginning.
- **When To Use This**:
    + When you need to track down a specific change. 
    + When you need to find who committed a specific change.
    + When you need to keep track of a feature/implementation that someone else is working on.

### New `git` commands

By default, you have been working on a `main` branch for your personal repository.

- This branch exists *locally*; your own directory (within the container environment) has these files.
- This branch also exists *remotely* on GitHub's servers.
- Since you have been the only one making changes (presumably from the Docker container), all the commits have flowed from *local copy* to *remote copy on GitHub*. No need to synchronize any work.

Now that you are collaborating on a project with others, we will need to adapt our workflow as follows:

- Treat `main` *on the remote* as a heavily guarded ground truth.
    + Only put changes in here by merging commits through *pull requests*.
    + Keep this in a working state as much as possible. That means others should be able to use it as a *branching point* to implement a new feature or discrete task.
    + This branch represents your final product.
- Each individual member works on a separate branch to avoid conflicts on `main`.
    + You work locally, not directly on GitHub, so make sure everyone starts with a `git pull` to retrieve the copy on GitHub.
    + Now that you own a copy of `main` on your machine, you can `git branch` to create your own working version to develop.
    + Make commits on your own branch, push it to GitHub, then create a pull request to merge your work onto `main`.

#### `git pull`

- The `git push` command moves commits from your *local repository* to a *remote repository*.
- The `git pull` command does the opposite; moves from the *remote* to your *local* repository.
- If you make commits on the *remote* and *local* separately, you're going to have a bad time... Be disciplined and only make edits on your machine (don't use the GitHub interface).
- **When To Use This**:
    + This should be the very first thing you do each time you sit down to work on your project.
    + Use it periodically during a session if you need to keep track of other changes.
    + When you need to see your collaborator's changes to test locally.

#### `git branch`

- See what the available branches are with `git branch`.
- To create a new branch *locally*, use `git branch my-branch-name`.
    + Until you push it to GitHub, that branch exists exclusively on your machine. No one can see that work yet.
- To work on your branch, you must `git checkout my-branch-name`.
    + Verify the branch you're on before making any edits or commits; e.g. `git branch` or `git status`.
    + If you make edits on the wrong branch, use `git stash` to safely store them away (before creating a commit), switch to the correct branch, then `git stash pop`.
- Avoid `git merge` to synchronize your work to `main`! Use pull requests instead.
    + If you use an AI tool to help you with `git`, let it know that you're using a branching model and only synchronize work through pull requests.

## Class Exercises

### Getting Started

1. Create a new repo.
    + Only one person needs to do this.
    + Add your partners as collaborators using the GitHub interface.
2. Clone the repository using `git clone`.
2. Each person should create a new local branch (use different names!)
    + Be sure to switch to the new branch.
3. Add a file or two to your branch and practice merging to the main branch.
    + Use a pull request for merging only!
4. Test what happens when your remote repository is ahead of your local repository, but you already staged new changes.

### Merge Conflicts

1. One team member adds a file `team.md` containing the line `Our project is about: TBD` and merges it into `main` through a pull request.
    + Everyone else should `git checkout main` and `git pull` to retrieve the file.
2. On your own branch, replace `TBD` with your own description of the project. Commit and push your branch.
    + Each team member should write something different on the *same line*.
3. Each team member opens a pull request into `main`. Merge only one of them.
    + Check the remaining pull requests on GitHub. Each should now report a conflict.
4. Each team member with a conflicting pull request resolves it locally on their own branch:
    a. Retrieve the updated `main` with `git checkout main` and `git pull`.
    b. Switch back with `git checkout my-branch-name`, then bring in the changes with `git merge main`.
    c. Run `git status` to see which files are in conflict, then open `team.md`.
    d. Edit the file to the version your team wants and delete the `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>` marker lines.
    e. `git add team.md`, `git commit`, and `git push`.
5. Refresh your pull request on GitHub and merge it.
    + Merge pull requests one at a time. Each merge may create a new conflict for the pull requests still open; repeat step 4 as needed.
    + Merging `main` *into your branch* is fine. Changes only go *into `main`* through pull requests.
6. Use `git log --oneline --decorate --graph --all` to find where the branches were joined.

### Forgetting to pull first

1. One team member creates a file on their branch and merges it into `main` through a pull request.
2. Everyone else does **not** `git pull`. Instead, each edits `README.md` on their local `main`, commits, and tries `git push`.
    + Read the error message. Why does `git` reject the push?
3. Recover by moving the commit onto a branch:
    a. `git branch readme-fix-yourname` to save your commit on a new branch.
    b. `git fetch`, then `git reset --hard origin/main` so local `main` matches GitHub.
    c. `git checkout readme-fix-yourname` and `git merge main` to bring in the newly merged work.
    d. `git push -u origin readme-fix-yourname` and open a pull request.
    + Only use `git reset --hard` after your commits are saved on another branch. It discards uncommitted changes.
4. Repeat with a different team member merging first, but this time the others create a new branch from their out-of-date `main` and push it.
    + Check whether the newly merged file appears on the new branch.
5. Always start a new task with `git checkout main`, `git pull`, and then `git branch new-branch-name`.

### Using stash

1. On `main`, edit a file but do not commit. Use `git status` to confirm you are on the wrong branch.
    a. `git stash` to set your changes aside. Verify with `git status` that the working tree is clean.
    b. `git checkout my-branch-name`, then `git stash pop` to restore the changes.
    c. Commit the changes on your branch.
2. One team member merges a pull request that changes `README.md`. Meanwhile, everyone else edits the same file on their local `main` without committing, then runs `git pull`.
    a. Note the error. `git` will not overwrite your uncommitted changes.
    b. `git stash`, `git pull`, then `git stash pop`.
    c. If `git stash pop` reports a conflict, resolve it as in the Merge Conflicts exercise, then run `git stash drop`. After a conflict, `git` keeps the stash until you drop it.
3. Practice managing several stashes:
    a. Create a new, untracked file and run `git stash`. Check whether the new file was stashed, then try `git stash -u`.
    b. Make two labeled stashes with `git stash push -m "first"` and `git stash push -m "second"`.
    c. View them with `git stash list` and restore one with `git stash pop stash@{1}`.
